entries.title: War's Mounting Toll
entries.content:
Today’s notice: The U.S. death toll rises in the Iran war. Maine’s Troy Jackson heads to the Democratic nomination. The U.S. Senate’s focus isn’t legislation. And: How Republicans are campaigning on the housing bill Trump called a “big yawn.”

THE LATEST

Three U.S. service members engaged in the Iran war were killed in action in two separate incidents over the weekend, and U.S. Central Command is trying to verify whether remains discovered near the site of one attack, in Jordan, match a fourth service member who was considered missing.

A total of 17 U.S. service members have died and dozens have been injured since the start of the war. As the escalation continues — last night marked nine consecutive days of U.S. strikes on Iran — it remains unclear how the rise in the death toll may sway public sentiment and congressional support. Most Americans already disapprove of the war.

Top congressional leaders offered their condolences, but delivered mixed messages on what should happen with the ongoing war. Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Arkansas) said President Donald Trump “is right to unleash hell on [the service members’] killers” while Sen. Mark Warner (D-Virginia) and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries called for de‑escalation.

“No more American heroes need to die because of this reckless war of choice,” Jeffries said on X.

Trump, on his way back to the White House from attending the World Cup final in New Jersey, said the U.S. strikes against Iran on Sunday night would be in honor of those fallen service members.

“We feel very badly but you know those great people, those great patriots were out there fighting that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump told reporters on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews. “We hit them very hard again tonight.”

Open tabs: Federal Agents Were Told F.B.I. Will No Longer Investigate ICE Confrontations (NYT); Trump immigration officials seek to mend frayed ties with business as arrests spike (WaPo); Trump praises Burnham over plans to fast-track North Sea oil (Telegraph); Russia pounds Kyiv in major ballistic missile attack (Reuters); 'Happy and healthy': JD and Usha Vance welcome fourth child (USA Today)

From the campaign trail

The Democratic field in Maine dramatically thinned out over the weekend, as Troy Jackson effectively clinched the nomination for U.S. Senate. As counties chose their delegates for this Saturday’s official nominating convention, more than half of those selected said they backed Jackson, Jenna reports.

Before Jackson became the presumptive nominee, Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said she was exiting the race to focus on her role as the state’s chief election officer amid Trump’s attacks on ballot integrity. Later Sunday, former state CDC Director Nirav Shah and former Capitol Hill staffer Jordan Wood also dropped out and immediately endorsed Jackson. Shah said he stepped aside because “the Democratic Party must be unified” to beat Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine).

Advice for Republicans campaigning on the big housing bill: “You could talk about the policy. You don't have to talk about how it became law,” a GOP strategist told NOTUS’ Raymond Fernández. Raymond dives into the emerging awkward situation for purple-district Republicans: They have a big, bipartisan bill on a topic Americans care about, but the head of their party called it a “big yawn” and refused to sign it.

“I don’t speak for the president,” Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R- Pennsylvania) told Raymond. “I know my voters, my constituents. My electors are super excited about the package.”

From the Hill

How the Senate stopped being the Senate, in charts. The numbers don’t lie: Nomination confirmations made up less than 20% of total roll-call votes prior to 2013 — the year then-Majority Leader Harry Reid nuked the filibuster for most nominations. By the end of 2024, nominations topped 60% of roll-call votes. NOTUS’ Avani Kalra crunched the numbers on how the World’s Greatest Deliberative Body has morphed into the world’s additional arena for partisan squabbles. The bottom line: More and more legislation is done through party-line reconciliation votes, and more and more floor time is devoted to confirmations.

NOTUS METRO

Sign up for our local newsletter. NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for all the latest, launching today!

Local news. Will Free Buses Ever Arrive in D.C.? By Zara Norman

Sports desk. Josiah Gray Still Wants to Help the Nats. Maybe Even This Year. By Jesse Dougherty

NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

Is Pennsylvania governor (and likely 2028 Democratic presidential candidate) Josh Shapiro actually good at governing? At NOTUS Perspectives, two local reporters chronicle his setbacks in Pennsylvania. Plus: The Reflecting Pool may have turned green, and the state fair may have been a dud, but Trump’s Garden of American Heroes is a great idea, argues Ben Jacobs.

NEW ON NOTUS

Clocking the daylight saving time effort in the Senate. “It’s got a lot of opposition,” Majority Leader John Thune told NOTUS’ Al Weaver. Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Arkansas) has pledged to stand in the way of this idea for as long as time itself.

That’s a stark outlook compared to the House. Rep. Scott DesJarlais (R-Tennessee) played the Beatles’ “Here Comes the Sun” as he presided over the floor during the chamber’s vote to make daylight saving time permanent last week. The bill passed 308-117.

But the cynicism in the House is palpable when it comes to the Senate. Members have seen their colleagues on the other side of the Capitol squash too many of their legislative dreams to predict when Americans won’t have to change their clocks twice a year. “They’ve all gone to the Sizzler for the early-bird special. They wanted to get to the fondue bar. So I don't know,” Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tennessee) told Manuela of when a bill could pass.

More: Trump’s Election-Tampering Claims Fall Flat, Including With Republicans, by Angie Orellana Hernandez

Ralph Norman Announces Campaign to Fill Lindsey Graham’s Vacant Seat, by Angie Orellana Hernandez

NOT US

  • Inside Trump’s Rush Job to Build His Arch, by Janay Kingsberry for The Atlantic
  • The U.S. Saw an Investment Boom in Venezuela. Now It’s a $37 Billion Problem. By Kejal Vyas and Ryan Dubé for The Wall Street Journal
  • Judges Ask Congress for Power to Fix Crumbling Courthouses, by Mattathias Schwartz for The New York Times

WEEK AHEAD

Today

Andy Burnham is expected to take over as U.K. prime minister.

Tuesday

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Joint Chiefs of Staff Chair John Caine and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins appear at a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing on the reconciliation budget plan.

House Oversight subcommittee hearing on the Smithsonian’s presentation of American history.

Filing opens for the South Carolina special Republican primary.

Wednesday

House Judiciary subcommittee hearing on Delaney Hall ICE detention facility.

U.N. Ambassador Mike Waltz testifies before the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

Thursday

House’s scheduled final day in session before August recess.

Trump hosts the LA Dodgers, last year’s World Series champions.

Brian Johnson’s confirmation hearing to be chair of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau before the Senate Banking Committee.

Candidates vying to replace Graham Platner in Maine participate in a televised debate.

Friday

Trump’s 10% global tariffs are due to expire.

Rescheduled White House Correspondents’ Dinner.

Saturday 

Maine Democratic Party hosts a nominating convention to replace Platner on the ballot.

entries.title: Will Free Buses Ever Arrive in D.C.?
entries.summary: Janeese Lewis George wants to make the metrobus free for residents on SNAP, but that "doesn’t need to be where we end."
entries.content:
Janeese Lewis George, who is all but sure to become the D.C.’s next mayor, wants to make the Metrobus free for recipients of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.

“A bus system that’s free for people on SNAP would mean residents in all eight wards, no matter their economic status or background, would be able to get to jobs, grocery stores, medical appointments, community gatherings, and social events,” her campaign told NOTUS in a statement.

If that comes to pass, Lewis George won’t rule out eventually expanding “the universe of people receiving free transit” if and when revenue is available.

“I see SNAP recipients as a good place to start but it doesn’t need to be where we end,” her campaign wrote.

It’s not the first time the District has floated free bus access for residents, more than 70% of whom already evade the fare, a Metro board member said during a May meeting. Mayor Muriel Bowser once made the Circulator service free, but that didn’t stick.

The city already offers kids free rides and gives discounts to government employees and those receiving SNAP. Neighboring cities like Baltimore and Alexandria, Virginia, have figured out how to make buses free for all residents — so, why not D.C.?

For starters, Alexandria and Baltimore receive state money to operate their buses, while the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority is a multistate agency without a dedicated revenue stream. When D.C. Council member Charles Allen, chair of the District’s transportation committee, proposed a monthly $100 credit on every D.C. resident’s Metro card in 2022 to fund city transit, Maryland and Virginia nixed the idea.

Allen’s bill passed without the credit, but did implement 24-hour bus service. He told NOTUS that he had hoped the credit could remedy D.C.’s “upside down” transit-benefit system.

“The overwhelming majority of people with transit benefits have high-paying jobs,” he said. “The majority of low-wage workers do not have a transit subsidy.”

That’s the demographic Lewis George is targeting with her proposal, which her campaign told NOTUS does not yet have a revenue source. Still, Allen called the idea “incredibly achievable” given that SNAP recipients already get a 50% discount.

Some transportation advocates argue that free buses should not be the focus of transportation reform. Alex Baca, the D.C. policy director at Greater Greater Washington, said increasing bus frequency and reliability are better targets.

“It doesn’t really matter if the bus is free if it doesn’t show up,” she told NOTUS.

Though bus fares accounted for 10% of WMATA’s total passenger revenue in the first quarter of fiscal year 2026, the agency says fares are a key part of its ability to deliver services. Fare evasion leads to around $50 million in lost revenue annually, Metro estimates.

While Metrobus ridership has largely recovered since the COVID-19 pandemic, fare payment has not. The bus saw 10.4 million boardings in May, but only one in four of those trips were paid for. Compare that with May 2019: 10.9 million boardings, but three in four trips paid for.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/yr9mj/2/To boost revenue, WMATA introduced a policy in May requiring bus drivers to quote the fare as riders board. Operators aren’t happy.

“Chasing down fare evaders isn't going to solve the systemic budget shortfalls that WMATA or other systems in the country face,” said Ben Lynn, a spokesperson for the local union representing more than 15,000 regional transit workers.

Quoting the fare can lead to disputes, which sometimes end in violence, Lynn said. D.C. recorded 152 assaults on bus operators this past fiscal year and 194 the year prior, according to data a WMATA spokesperson shared with NOTUS.

Al Clements, an operator who lives in southeast D.C. but drives Alexandria’s DASH bus, almost quit his job after one such confrontation. It was 2017, and he’d just quoted a rider the fare.

“He talked to me real crazy, he called me all kinds,” Clements said. “We was going down the road, and he just kept verbally abusing me. Sitting right there in that first seat.”

Since DASH went fare-free in 2021, Clements said he doesn’t have to worry about riders getting embarrassed or agitated and confronting him.

“It went from ‘F you,’ and ‘you an A-hole’ to ‘I appreciate you,’ ‘thank you,’” Clements said. “It makes the job a lot more tolerable.”
_C0A4629 copy.jpg (7396x4930, AR: 1.50)DASH ridership has increased from 3.77 million boardings in 2019 to 5.67 million last year. Assaults on bus operators have fallen “dramatically” in that time, said Raymond Mui, DASH’s chief infrastructure and development officer. There were two incidents recorded last year, as compared to nine in 2022.

“We made public transit as easy to use and as carefree to use as a public sidewalk, or as an elevator, or as a park, or as a library,” Mui told NOTUS.

But going fare-free didn’t come at the expense of frequency or reliability, Mui said. The city has been able to get people on and off the bus much faster, meaning the bus travels faster, too.

“We were able to speed our buses up, increase our services and get more bang for the buck for the community,” Mui said.

Alexandria is a fraction of D.C.’s size and serves a fraction of its population, but leaders in the District think there’s a way to eventually roll out free access citywide. The route to that reality will begin if and when Lewis George is sworn in and makes her push to bring free transit to SNAP recipients.

“It’s absolutely a goal that she and I share,” Allen said. “It’s something I want to do. It’s something we’ve been working on different ways to get at.”

entries.title: Trump Undercut Republicans’ Campaign Message on Housing
entries.summary: “You could talk about the policy,” said one Republican operative. “You don’t have to talk about how it became law.”
entries.content:
President Donald Trump’s refusal to sign the housing bill passed by Congress has turned into a complicated political question for Republicans: How do you campaign on a legislative win that was rejected by the head of your party?

The legislation, which is the most significant housing package to come out of Congress in more than three decades and represents one of the biggest legislative victories of the year for Republicans, became law this month despite the president’s inaction. It’s making for some hard conversations with the voters, who are very attuned to the cost of living.

“[Housing is] one of the number one asks I have in my district,” Rep. Zach Nunn (R- Iowa) told NOTUS of issues constituents asked Congress to work on. “If the president didn’t want to sign it, that’s over to the president.”

“I’m glad that we stood firm and we had a veto-proof majority. And sometimes Republicans have to stand up to the president and say, ‘This is what our districts need.’”

The president endorsed several versions of the bill, including its final form. But he ultimately refused to sign it, saying instead that the Save America Act was the administration’s top priority and should be Congress’ too.

“I don’t speak for the president,” Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R- Pennsylvania), who represents a swing district that could help determine control of the House next year, told NOTUS when asked whether he believed voters would credit Republicans for the policy despite Trump’s calling the bill “a big yawn” relative to election security.

“I know my voters, my constituents. My electors are super excited about the package,” Bresnahan said.

The housing bill is aimed at fast-tracking housing development across the nation by removing some environmental and construction review standards and expanding how existing federal programs administered by the Department of Housing and Urban Development use funds for construction. It also limits the number of single-family homes institutional investors can own.

Every step of passing the bill was a headache for Republicans. It got caught up in a monthslong standoff between the House and Senate. Some Republicans griped about the outsize role Democrats took in negotiating the package, which in the end passed with broad bipartisan support. And Trump oscillated in his support for at least one of the provisions in the bill.

Now, the careful dance Republicans have to do around it on the campaign trail has become another in a long line of headaches, when they’d widely expected an easy-to-sell legislative feat.

“Every House Republican can claim that they fought to have this bill passed because they voted for it, and so you know they’re the ones running, not President Trump,” a Republican operative told NOTUS, adding that the package is not the only affordability policy Republicans should message on. “You could talk about the policy. You don't have to talk about how it became law.”

Some Republicans running for reelection are doing exactly that.

Sarah Chamberlain, president of the Republican Main Street Partnership — a conservative nonprofit that nearly a hundred sitting lawmakers are part of — told NOTUS that Republicans' messaging on the package should be “localized” and that lawmakers should keep talking about “the fact that they voted, they passed the bill, and it became law.”

“The members of Main Street are back in their districts talking about the importance of this legislation and how it affects your day-to-day life. They’re not mentioning what the president said,” Chamberlain said.

Both Republican operatives told NOTUS that they believed people outside of D.C. are not aware of the president’s comments or his refusal to sign the bill.

Asked about Republican messaging on the legislation and Trump’s refusal to sign it, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pennsylvania) said the bill was a “huge” bipartisan policy win “on probably the most important aspect of affordability, which is housing.”

Pressed about the president’s role, Fitzpatrick — who holds another key seat the Republicans are trying to hold on to in order to keep the majority — said the president’s opinions were “his.”

“Overwhelming numbers of Democrats, Republicans in the House and Senate voted for it. Everybody’s got to be accountable for our actions,” Fitzpatrick said.

The White House did not respond to NOTUS’ request for comment.

Housing is a key part of the affordability conversation both parties say they want to address. The U.S. is currently facing a shortage of more than 5 million homes, according to Pew Research Center. A Gallup poll conducted in May found that only 25% of non-homeowners believe they will be able to buy a home in the next five years — the lowest percentage in more than a decade.

In the fight for control of the lower chamber, Democrats have also been campaigning on the bill. The day the president canceled the signing ceremony, more than 20 Democratic lawmakers held a rally outside the Capitol to demand the president to sign the legislation and accused him of holding it hostage.

Now, vulnerable House Republicans are downplaying that the bill became law without Trump’s signature.

“I’m less worried about the process and more about the actual specifics of the bill,” Rep. Mike Lawler (R-New York), who is running in a district won by former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, told NOTUS. He touted the bill as a Republican-led effort.

Some Republicans are even choosing not to speak about the package at all.

When asked about the bill and the president, Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colorado) said: “Oh, well, let’s back up even before that. Let’s go back to the Working Families Tax Cut.”

entries.title: Josiah Gray Still Wants to Help the Nats. Maybe Even This Year.
entries.summary: Once the face of the Nationals’ rebuild, the 28-year-old pitcher is nearing a comeback after two years of injury rehab.
entries.content:
For a while there, all Nationals fans had to get excited about were debuts. Or, to parrot the social media hype machine, all they had to get excited about were DEBUTS. There was Keibert Ruiz and CJ Abrams, MacKenzie Gore and Cade Cavalli, Jackson Rutledge and Brady House, James Wood and Dylan Crews, DJ Herz and Robert Hassell III, Daylen Lile and Jake Irvin.

For the darkest days, there was Blake Rutherford.

For the waiver nerds, Alex Call.

For the sickest of sickos, Jake Alu.

But before all of them was Josiah Gray, who debuted for the Nats on Aug. 2, 2021 — when, maybe more than ever, fans needed a sign that things might eventually be OK again (heavy emphasis on might). Three days earlier, he had arrived in the Max Scherzer-Trea Turner trade, which had capped a deadline fire sale that saw eight veterans go out and 12 unproven players come in. Gray was, in turn, the roster’s first public face of the rebuild. And because of that, he would answer so many questions about patience, about sticking with a broken club, about what it would take for an odd collection of dreamers and has-beens to eventually play respectable baseball.

Sign up for our Metro Newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

And he pitched, of course, at one point so well that he was an All Star in 2023. And then he basically disappeared.

“Man, where to even begin …” Gray said to me over the phone last week. He picked up the call from South Florida, where he’s spent the better part of the last two years and three months, stretching and throwing and eating quiet breakfasts at the Nationals’ team facility, marooned. Because for that entire time, he’s been trying to get back from injury, first with a long recovery from Tommy John surgery, now after a devastating setback at the end of spring training. He last pitched in the majors on April 4, 2024, when some of the fielders behind him were Joey Gallo, Jesse Winker, Trey Lipscomb and Ildemaro Vargas.

But after throwing off a bullpen mound in West Palm Beach on July 10, Gray, 28, feels closer to a return than he has in a good while.

“When it’s been this long, it can be hard not to feel like you’re forgotten about,” Gray said. “But that’s one of the things that you just try to not let build up in your head. I’m trying to have a fresh mindset and put all the work in behind the scenes, so that when my name is called I’m ready. I mean, it’s been time to make new baseball memories.”

One big question, should Gray keep progressing, is if he can still fit into the Nats’ future, especially with a whole new front office and coaching staff. And another is how different a pitcher he might be if he gets back to a major league mound.

After missing the first half of 2024 with elbow and forearm strains, Gray underwent Tommy John surgery that July. He rehabbed for the rest of that season, then all of 2025, finishing that year with three short appearances in the minors. The goal was to compete to reclaim his rotation spot this spring, which resulted in the team telling him he needed some more time. He was optioned to Triple-A Rochester in late March. The plan was for him to start during the Red Wings’ opening series in Jacksonville. But then, during a final tune-up in West Palm Beach, his elbow didn’t feel right. Tests revealed another flexor strain, the same issue that first slowed him down two years before. It was straight back to the injured list.

“I was so close to escaping that rehab mindset,” Gray said. “You know, that was a tough one.”

No cliché is off limits when you’ve spent more than two years rehabbing your arm, far away from your teammates, worlds away from your major league life. And so Gray uses a lot of them. He is just stacking one good day on top of another. He has learned a lot about himself. He is enjoying the process, at least as best he can, and appreciating how many people are invested in getting him back to the show. That’s no small thing, he says. It is its own kind of blessing.

But none of that means there isn’t a real, aching itch to help the Nats however he can. They have been short on arms all year, cycling through options in a tortured effort to find the 27 outs needed to win. And Gray is also eager to work more with the new staff, which is much more data-minded than his previous coaches in D.C.

Gray has always pored over his metrics, the kind of guy who throws a pitch in the bullpen and immediately turns to an iPad to look at how it spun and moved. At his best, he’s ridden his plus slider as much as possible, working it off four-seam fastballs at the top of the zone. At his worst, those high fastballs have been way too friendly to power hitters, which is why he led the league in homers allowed in 2022 and part of why underlying numbers have never considered him a top-of-the-rotation arm. But in 2023, his All-Star year, he performed above average across six months, showing that, before the injuries, he could have contributed to a winning club.

When he talks about doing that now, Gray says it could be as a starter, as a reliever, whatever is needed for a Nationals team that’s still overachieving at 50-50. He expects to have a better idea of how he’s changed — or, ideally, how he hasn’t — once he pitches in minor league games in the near future, which would be the next step in his comeback.

But until then, he’ll stay in the same routine for at least a bit longer. He’ll show up at the facility between 8 and 9 a.m. He’ll eat his breakfast, warm his arm with plyo balls and then work off the mound. Then, back at home, he’ll hang with his wife and their dog, Cowboy, an Australian shepherd. He might fire up the grill. And then they’ll probably turn on the Nationals game.

“I wish I was a bigger part of it,” Gray said. “But with time left in the year, I think I could still make an impact.”

entries.title: The Senate Is Working More on Party-Line Nominations — and Less on Legislation
entries.summary: The decades-long Senate trend toward less legislating is the result of extreme partisanship.
entries.content:
The Senate is known as the world’s greatest deliberative body, but lately it’s not debating much and is largely holding party-line votes on nominees for the administration and the judiciary, a NOTUS review of Senate voting patterns shows.

NOTUS examined hundreds of roll-call votes taken in 2021 and 2022 under a Democratic trifecta and in 2025 and 2026 in Republican-controlled Washington and found that the Senate is voting more frequently on Cabinet and judicial appointments than on legislation, regardless of the party in power.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/yrPfs/3/Data from the Congressional Research Service shows that nominations made up less than 20% of the total roll-call votes prior to 2013, when the Senate lowered the threshold to a simple majority for most federal judges and executive branch nominations. By the end of 2024, that number topped 60%.

“There has been a decades-long transformation of [the Senate],” Casey Burgat, a politics professor at George Washington University, said. “There's been a huge atrophying of the lawmaking power of individual senators and of the Senate as a whole.”

Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois), the Democratic whip who has served in the Senate for nearly 30 years, told NOTUS that the increased focus on nominations has detracted from legislating.

“It’s gotten to the point where we spend most of our time talking about nominations,” Durbin said.

Gregory Koger, a political scientist who studies the Senate’s 60-vote voting threshold, the filibuster, said that greater polarization is responsible for the meltdown in the Senate’s ability to pass laws. The number of competitive seats across the country has shrunk to historic lows, according to the Cook Political Report.

Lawmakers no longer have to compete as aggressively for moderate voters or members of the opposing party, and bipartisan collaboration has become a liability rather than an asset in tenuous primaries, Koger added.

“Increasingly there's a downside risk from an angry, disappointed partisan base, on both sides, for compromising,” he said.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia), who chairs the Senate Republican Policy Committee, agreed, telling NOTUS that bipartisanship has declined throughout her nearly 12 years in the upper chamber.

“There’s certain issues that we can go bipartisan, but most recently, even those are getting shut down. Everything is about a political advantage,” Capito said.

Senators are instead spending more time voting on partisan proposals offered by the minority party. The NOTUS review of roll-call votes found that Senate Democrats have forced more than 30% of the roll-call votes in 2026 –– up from under 20% in 2025, which was similar to the number of Republican-forced votes under Democratic control.

“Your whole goal is to make them look bad,” Burgat said. “To not help, to obstruct, because that's what your voters want. It helps you as a party maintain a better electoral strategy heading into campaign season, and it's always campaign season.”
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/zzgVq/5/Work on bipartisan legislation has been steadily decreasing since 2009. Republicans, then led by Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky), decided it would be politically advantageous to block any legislation and nominees proposed by then-President Barack Obama.

That strategy was followed by a change in the Senate’s nomination process, lowering the 60-vote threshold to a simple majority vote for most federal judicial nominees. Later, Republicans eliminated the filibuster for nominees to the Supreme Court.

In 2025, Senate Republicans voted to make it easier to confirm executive branch nominees in groups under a simple majority. Senate Majority Leader John Thune announced in April that the Senate had nearly cleared President Donald Trump’s nominations backlog and that leadership was set to begin a four-week push to confirm more before summer recess in August.

“It’s not like that then makes the Senate more efficient so it has more time to legislate,” Koger said. “It’s mostly so they can approve more nominations.”
Donald Trump,John Thune (4908x3272, AR: 1.50)A decline in bipartisanship has also led to both Democratic and Republican majorities legislating more aggressively through the budget reconciliation process over the past two decades. The maneuver allows leadership to bypass the Senate’s 60-vote filibuster and pass tax and spending priorities primarily along partisan lines.

The Senate has voted on five approved reconciliation bills since 2017 and 12 in total since 2001, including two so far this year alone. The upper chamber passed its first major party-line bill in 1980 and passed only nine over the following two decades, according to the Senate’s list of “vote-a-ramas.”

Steven Smith, a political scientist who studies the Senate, told NOTUS that today’s expanded use of the reconciliation tool began back in 2001, when congressional Republicans employed the process to pass the first wave of tax cuts under then-President George W. Bush.

“It's gradually blossomed into one or more reconciliation bills carrying the bulk of a president's agenda,” Smith said. “Between reconciliation, appropriations and nominations, you get a very big chunk of the roll-call voting record in the Senate.”

Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-New Hampshire), a moderate Democrat who has led bipartisan negotiations on issues like infrastructure, health care and foreign policy since she joined the Senate in 2009, told NOTUS that she’s seen a breakdown in good-faith talks on Capitol Hill because of the uptick in party-line bills.

“It is not a good way to approach getting things done around here,” Shaheen said. “It becomes very, by design, partisan. It doesn’t allow for debate and for working together.”

The expanded use of party-line legislating has contributed to the declining power of the Senate’s committees. In years past, individual senators from both parties negotiated legislation in groups behind closed doors. Now, Senate leadership drives bills forward, injecting a more partisan lens to the process.

“Ultimately the [outcome] of these monster reconciliation bills, that try to impose as much of the president's program as possible, is that it limits the number of members who have a meaningful role in designing public policy,” Smith said.

Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa), the president pro tempore of the Senate, where he has served for more than 45 years, pushed back on the assertion that the number of party-line bills has increased. He said reconciliation has always been the go-to when it doesn’t seem like a bill can get to 60 votes.

“As far as reconciliation, it hasn’t changed much,” Grassley told NOTUS. “I think we've had ‘vote-a-ramas’ ever since I can remember." Vote-a-ramas are a long series of amendment votes tied to reconciliation bills.

Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wisconsin), who is in line to take over as chair of the Senate Budget Committee following the death of Lindsey Graham, said that he expects the upper chamber will continue to use the maneuver.
U.S. Congress (4850x3233, AR: 1.50)“It’s probably going to be the only tool because Democrats are completely obstructionist and being obnoxious and not doing what’s in the best interests of the nation,” Johnson said.

But the scope of what is included in those spending bills has expanded. For example, Senate Republicans funded the Department of Homeland Security using reconciliation after bipartisan negotiations to fund the agency fell apart. According to the Congressional Research Service, it was the first time senators replaced the traditional appropriations process with a party-line bill after they couldn’t secure funding for certain government agencies.

The unraveling of the appropriations process followed two of the longest government shutdowns in history and could drive majorities even further toward partisan funding efforts. Appropriations measures are still considered some of the few must-pass bipartisan bills and are negotiated in committee.

“That is not how it works,” Durbin said about bypassing committees for party-line bills. “We’ve ended up with a situation virtually where it’s used for everything. We’ve pushed the lever way too much.”

entries.title: Regional Fights Stall Daylight Saving Time Bill's Senate Chances
entries.summary: “It’s got a lot of opposition,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) told NOTUS.
entries.content:
There’s a whole lot of daylight between the House and the Senate — literally.

The House voted last week to make daylight saving time permanent, marking the latest congressional foray into the decades-old battle over whether the U.S. should change the clocks twice a year.

But despite the sizable bipartisan vote, the bill — known as the Sunshine Protection Act — is showing few signs of making headway across the Capitol, with scores of senators representing Midwestern and northern states lining up against it.

“I think it’s pretty strong,” Sen. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota) said of the level of opposition, adding that the bill’s prospect of passage is dim.

While many issues fall along party lines, the fault lines in the fight over daylight saving vs. standard time are largely geographic. While coastal states would be the beneficiaries of a full year with more daylight later in the day, midwestern and mountain states would feel more impacts.

The lack of sun in the early morning hours when children are leaving for school in the morning is a chief concern.

Under permanent daylight saving time, cities along the westernmost parts of the eastern, central and mountain time zones would not see the sun rise in the winter until later in the morning. Some cities, including Pierre, S.D., and South Bend, Ind., would not see the sun until after 9 a.m. on some days.

“Have you ever seen any issue that people are more passionate about and that divides the country more by region than that one?” Senate Majority Leader John Thune told NOTUS about changing the current system. “It’s got a lot of opposition.”

Leading the charge is Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton, the No. 3 Senate Republican, who has made clear he would block any attempt to pass the House bill via unanimous consent.

The effort to lock the clock in favor of daylight saving has been a windy road in recent years. A bill backed by former Sen. Marco Rubio (R-Florida) passed somewhat surprisingly with a unanimous vote in 2022.

Cotton revealed in a floor speech last year that he did not object at that time because there was a “miscommunication,” as he expected another senator to do so. He also said he had not “adequately communicated to my staff the depth of my opposition” to the measure.

The bill died in the House.

Proponents of daylight saving once tried again to pass it unanimously last year, but Cotton blocked it, arguing they were trying to put “a sunny face” on the proposal.

More than a dozen senators from both parties have voted against the daylight saving shift recently in the Senate Commerce Committee: Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Delaware), Ted Budd (R-North Carolina), Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois), Deb Fischer (R-Nebraska), Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota), Jerry Moran (R-Kansas), Gary Peters (D-Michigan), Jacky Rosen (D-Nevada), Tim Sheehy (R-Montana), Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), Todd Young (R-Indiana), Thune and Wicker.

Even proponents of the measure don’t see a path at present.

“No, Tom Cotton’s going to block that,” Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama) said.

Tuberville also quipped that more daylight would give him more time on the golf course. When asked how many more rounds he’d get in, Tuberville laughed and conceded: “Quite a few.”

Also dooming the bill is that it would not allow individual states to opt out of permanent daylight time. They would have already needed to pass a bill to observe permanent standard time. The only two states to do that are Arizona and Hawaii.

“I just don’t think we want a mandate,” Thune said.

The push to lock the clock one way or another stems from the unpopularity of the pair of clock changes during the year. According to an AP-NORC poll taken in October, only 12 percent support the current system compared to 47 percent in opposition. Forty percent were neutral.

Congress passed a law establishing permanent daylight saving in the 1970s, but it was repealed less than a year later due to the dark mornings.

“In Minnesota, Michigan and the Dakotas, you’re going to have schoolchildren getting mowed over waiting for the school bus in the dark,” Wicker said. “I’m surprised the House passed it by such an overwhelming majority.”

Another thing standing in the way is the crowded to-do list on the Senate floor. Ahead of the August recess alone, the chamber is expected to deal with the nominations of acting Attorney General Todd Blanche to lead the Justice Department, Jay Clayton to become Director of National Intelligence and acting Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling to head the department full-time. Passing a larger package of lower-level nominations is also in the works.

The Senate is also hoping to move other items, including a reauthorization of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, a Russia sanctions package and a cryptocurrency regulatory bill. Further complicating the calendar is that memorial services for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-South Carolina) in Washington and his home state are slated for the end of July.

Amid the spirited debate, there are also members who simply don’t care one way or another.

“I don’t wake up or go to bed thinking about it. I know it’s religion for everybody … but it’s not religion for me,” said Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina). “Just tell me what time to set my clock.”
